lesson.title: From Rate to Amount: The First-Order Integrated Rate Law
lesson.summary: Turns the first-order rate law into a formula that predicts exactly how much reactant remains at any moment in time, using a natural logarithm to unwind the calculus of continuous decay.
lesson.body:
The rate law you already know for a first order reaction, rate = k[A], tells you how fast the reaction is going at one instant, for one particular concentration. It does not, by itself, tell you what concentration remains after 10 minutes, or how long you need to wait for 90 percent of the reactant to disappear. Those are the practical questions a chemist actually needs answered in a lab, in a chemical plant, or in a pharmacology study. The trouble is that rate is not constant. As [A] falls, the rate falls too, so you cannot just multiply "rate times time" the way you would for something moving at a constant speed. Getting from the differential rate law, which describes a rate that keeps changing, to a formula for concentration at any time t requires calculus, specifically integration, which is exactly why this family of equations is called the integrated rate law.

For a first order reaction, that integration produces a remarkably clean result:

ln[A] = ln[A]0 minus kt

where [A]0 is the initial concentration, [A] is the concentration remaining at time t, and k is the first order rate constant, with units of inverse time such as s^-1 or min^-1. You will often see it written as ln([A]/[A]0) = -kt, which is the same statement rearranged. Notice the shape: this is the equation of a straight line, y = mx + b, if you let y = ln[A], x = t, the slope m = -k, and the intercept b = ln[A]0. That structural fact becomes the entire basis for how chemists confirm experimentally that a reaction is first order, a story picked up later in this unit when we start plotting real data.

Here is a fully worked example. Suppose a first order reaction has a rate constant k = 0.0231 min^-1 and starts at [A]0 = 0.500 M. What concentration remains after 60.0 minutes?

Plug directly into the integrated rate law:
ln[A] = ln(0.500) minus (0.0231 min^-1)(60.0 min)
ln[A] = -0.693 minus 1.39
ln[A] = -2.08

To recover [A] itself, exponentiate both sides:
[A] = e^(-2.08) = 0.125 M

So after one hour, the concentration has fallen from 0.500 M to 0.125 M, exactly one quarter of the starting amount. That is not a coincidence. Once you meet half-life later in this unit, you will see that 60 minutes is exactly two half-lives for this particular value of k, and two half-lives always cuts a first order concentration to one quarter.

The natural logarithm shows up here for a specific physical reason, not just because it makes the algebra convenient. A first order process is one in which the rate of disappearance is directly proportional to how much is currently present, so the reaction always removes the same fraction of what remains in each unit of time, never the same absolute amount. That constant-fraction behavior is exactly the mathematical signature of exponential decay, the same pattern that governs radioactive decay, the elimination of a drug from the bloodstream, or the discharge of a capacitor. Recognizing "first order kinetics" as "exponential decay" is one of the most transferable ideas in this course. The integrated rate law you just derived is simply the algebraic fingerprint of that behavior, built directly on top of the differential first order rate law and the definition of a first order reaction that you already know.
